articles.title: The Live-Action Cyberpunk 2077 Movie Won't Retrace the Game's Steps, CD Projekt Confirms
articles.summary: CD Projekt Red has finally spoken up about the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie. The company said it doesn’t want to do a 1:1 adaptation of the game, instead telling a new story within the same universe.
articles.body:
CD Projekt Red has finally spoken up about the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie . The company said it doesn’t want to do a 1:1 adaptation of the game, instead telling a new story within the same universe.

"At this point, we can only say that we definitely don't want to make a film adaptation of the game," co-CEO Michał Nowakowski told Polish outlet PAP Biznes , via GamesRadar . "We want to tell a story in the world of Cyberpunk, but it won't be a one-to-one translation of the game's story."

The Cyberpunk movie is being created in partnership with Parmount, now under the Skydance banner after the recent merger . The film will be produced by Lorenzo di Bonaventura, of live-action Transformers fame.

It’ll be interesting to see how far the movie strays from the game, which featured a freelance mercenary called V who put a mysterious computer chip in their brain and ended up haunted by the digital ghost of Keanu Reeves’ Johnny Silverhand. I’d personally love them to go back, get Reeves back in, and tell Silverhand’s story before he ended up stuck in a chip.

Of course, the Cyberpunk universe — created by tabletop RPG designer Mike Pondsmith — is wide enough to tell a range of original stories. It’s fertile soil for pulling at themes of identity, autonomy, and the self as a ship of theseus to be modified and reprinted.

It sounds like a similar approach the company took to anime. Cyberpunk: Edgerunners feels like a faithful multimedia project within the world CDPR created — featuring locations and characters from the game world — but it tells a fresh story about original characters in its dystopian posthuman hellscape.

The Studio Trigger-led anime series is back on Netflix this month when Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 launches on October 20. Check out the IGN interview with the creators of Edgerunners for the lowdown.

CD Projekt also recently announced that work has officially begun on Project Hadar , its first game in its own original universe. The company has previously only played in the worlds of others, with The Witcher based on novels and Cyberpunk based on a tabletop RPG.

Elsewhere in CD Project Land, The Witcher 3 just got a remaster on consoles and PC, which saw the iconic RPG get a makeover. There were some issues with the new visuals, particularly heavy bloom in The Witcher 3 remaster , but CDPR was on the case quickly. And of course, Cyberpunk 2 is in the works, although it feels years away.

Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

articles.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
articles.summary: I never played Ocarina of Time, but 2 hours with the remake proves there’s so much more to this masterpiece than nostalgia.
articles.body:
No matter how much I wish it were the case, I’ll never know what it was like to have seen Jaws in the summer of 1975. Yet, I still get the joy of watching the film that changed blockbuster cinema forever 50 years later, whether that be on towering IMAX screens or wonderfully restored 4K blu-rays. The experience of being there when a film, game, or piece of music entered our culture and witnessing its impact firsthand can never be replicated, but through preservation, remasters, and remakes, new audiences get to uncover these treasures for themselves.

This is the case with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. My recent playtime with a demo of the Switch 2 remake felt like digital archaeology; the unearthing of a cultural artefact that informed so much of what came after it, while remaining a gleaming treasure in its own right. A link between one era of video games and another. A sacred text. At least, that’s how it felt to me. You see, I’ve never played the original.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Preview Screenshots

Well, that’s a tiny bit of a lie — I did briefly mess around in the opening hour or so of the 3DS port around a decade ago. I know, I should be subject to whatever form of medieval torture you deem appropriate. But the truth is, it’s one that simply passed me by, despite having played several Zeldas since — Tears of the Kingdom is a masterwork of open-world design in my eyes, even if Wind Waker still sits closest to my heart. I never owned a Nintendo 64, and likely got distracted by whatever was happening in my mid-20s, which made me put down Ocarina’s portable version. But now, finally, I’m ready to right my wrongs, and after playing two hours of the remake, I couldn’t be more excited to do so.

During my time with the 2026 version of Link’s most defining adventure, I got to play through Kokiri Forest, wander around Castle Town, and complete the Forest Temple. Even from this small sample size, I could see flashes of some of my favourite games within it, and the inspirational sparks it must have fired off into other game developers' minds in 1998. But most importantly, I had a ridiculously fun time with it. From just that short session, I can safely assure you that, if you’re like me and have also somehow let this piece of history slip through your fingers, there’s plenty here for newcomers to enjoy. When it launches in November, there will be little excuse to leave it unplayed.

“Anyone who makes 3D games who says they’ve not borrowed something from Mario or Zelda is lying — from the games on Nintendo 64, not necessarily the ones from today,” said Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser to the New York Times . It’s a point that’s hard to argue with, and one I wouldn’t dare contest — I think one of the minds behind GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 probably knows more about game design than I.

Nintendo having created something of a lending library for game design is something I could see most clearly in the Forest Temple. I enjoyed unpicking each of its knotted series of corridors and unpacking its hidden secrets, all wrapped in a spooky mansion setting. Every room is a puzzle, whether in the more traditional sense of moving heavy stone cubes around to unblock routes or navigating combat challenges that put your tool belt to the test.

Battles are never overly challenging but wonderfully engaging, with looming sword-and-shield-wielding skeletons reacting to your actions as you, in turn, have to counter theirs with a well-timed dodge or stun. When striking them down, you can see the basic structure that would go on to influence Batman Arkham’s brawls — one of the defining melee combat systems — in the way that fights carry the rhythm of enemies reading your movements and you, in turn, having to react with the correct rock-paper-scissors response.

Outside of scraps, the structure of the whole temple can’t help but conjure memories of Dark Souls' intertwining, shortcut-unlocking approach to level design. Every route loops back to its central chamber, in which four coloured flames need to be lit in order for the path to the boss to reveal itself. The construction of this area is masterfully done, clearly indicating what you have to achieve without ever holding your hand too much. That freedom of thought has always been prevalent in Zelda, all the way up to how Tears of the Kingdom brings out your most experimental thoughts with its building systems.

In Ocarina, breadcrumbs of clues as to how to achieve objectives are given, with tempting buttons placed out of reach behind locked gates and high up ledges seemingly unreachable. That’s until you realise you can rotate the hallways and alter the architecture of the temple completely, like some sort of prototype of Dishonored 2’s Clockwork Mansion. This mechanic is key to navigating the space, and where much of its challenge lies. Entire projects, such as Fez, have gone on to use a system like this to power a whole game. Here, it’s utilised for less than an hour. It’s a testament to the enduring inventiveness of Nintendo that these ideas still echo through gaming today.

I found great joy in the simplicity of the temple, but one that tickled my brain enough to never seem like child’s play. There’s a delicate balance when it comes to signposting without holding your hand, to the point where the temple delivered several “aha” moments over the course of my time exploring it. Some came naturally through decades of playing video games, like seeing a frozen target with a raging fire nearby, clearly indicating I needed to fire an arrow through the flames to melt it. But some did give me pause for thought, such as not realising I needed to use my bow to knock each of the temple’s four guardian sprites out of paintings in order to progress. Still, I tried it anyway, and lo and behold, it worked. It’s that sort of “let's see if this works” experimentation that I’ve always appreciated in Zelda, so it’s no surprise to see it pioneered here in the series first foray into 3D.

I was pleasantly surprised to see that the temple’s boss, Phantom Ganon, was also a puzzle, instead of a toe-to-toe fight. Some of my favourite bosses in all of gaming are enigmas to be solved rather than tests of reflexes, whether that be any of Shadow of the Colossus’ beasts or, perhaps more analogously here, Elden Ring’s Rennala. Brain over brawn is clearly Link’s preference too, with well-timed parries key to bringing down this foe once you work out which of the ones charging on horseback out of the paintings that surround you is real.

One of the more notable changes this remake introduces is a jump button. Link was grounded in the original Ocarina of Time, only able to hop over specific gaps dictated by his creators. It was a decision intended to create contrast between Nintendo’s two big series. “You had to press a button to jump when we first started making The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time,” explained Yoshiaki Koizumi, a designer on the original game and Nintendo’s current Senior Executive Officer and Direct host, in an Iwata Asks . “As we were making Super Mario 64, we were thinking about The Legend of Zelda the whole time, and started talking about decreasing the action element in The Legend of Zelda and increasing the puzzle elements.”

Modern Zelda, and modern adventure games in general, have tended to favour action over puzzles, so it’s somewhat natural that a jump has been introduced in the remake. It’s almost impossible not to think of Breath of the Wild, and its sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, when going back to any older Zelda now. This remake’s Link certainly controls similarly to how those most recent incarnations of Hyrule’s hero do. There’s a great sense of responsiveness to each of his actions, whether platforming or in combat, with the latter feeling very familiar. No great surprise really when, even 20 years later, Nintendo still utilised the same lock-on approach to duels. In fact, it was remarkable to me how second nature much of what I played in Ocarina of Time felt to me, considering I’d never explored the Forest Temple before. You can almost see through the code, one that has been comprehensively studied and iterated on by Nintendo, and practically every other game developer since.

Just as you can see the impact of Jaws rippling decades later in the likes of Jordan Peele's Nope or Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus One, Ocarina of Time can be felt in both the most recent Zeldas and adventure games in general. Of course, part of me always knew this. But as much as I enjoy those fantastic recent films, it's still Spielberg's shark hunt that stands tallest to me. It's remarkable how enjoyable these pieces of history still are today. It's far too early for me to know whether I'll feel the same way about Ocarina, but I’d be lying if I said the fact that I'm considering that after just a couple of hours hasn’t surprised me a little. I know this is a modern interpretation, but part of me expected this remake to feel slightly archaic; this is a nearly 30-year-old collection of ideas, after all. I was wrong. It feels full of freshly conjured magic.

Of course, Nintendo isn’t without its own inspirations. I realise 3D games were appearing on consoles such as the PlayStation years prior to Link making his N64 debut, and you can see flashes of them here. Perhaps I’m making decades-old observations here, but I enjoyed the way its twisting hallways resemble the original Resident Evil’s Spencer Mansion, rebuilt for an audience that likes to laugh in the face of horror rather than be chilled by it. You can see developers learning how to create explorable open spaces through time, from Capcom’s 1996 mansion, through Nintendo’s 1998 temple, to Rockstar’s 2001 Liberty City. It’s somewhat serendipitous, then, that Rockstar’s latest world, GTA 6’s Leonida, arrives just days after the Ocarina of Time remake. Two games of wildly different scope, but equally monumental. Digital archaeology prefacing a new age altogether.

I know that this game won't ever hold as special a place in my heart as it does for the millions who grew up with it, but there's still more than enough to make up for that. Just from this small sampling, I can tell it's an impeccably designed adventure that left me hungry to devour the full thing. If you’ve somehow let it slip as I did, I wouldn’t miss out this time around.

I’d never played Ocarina of Time before, yet, strangely, having played everything that it has come to inspire after, there was a comforting sense of familiarity. Now, I can’t wait to get my hands back on it and savour every moment of it for myself when it is released on November 5.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: The Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 Takes the Best PC Gaming Handheld and Adds OLED
articles.body:
Last year, Asus and Xbox worked together to launch the Asus ROG Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X , and the latter is still one of the best handheld gaming PCs on the market right now. Not only is is great at playing games, but even amid the RAMpocalypse, the Xbox Ally X hasn't gone up in price and will still cost the same $999 that it did back in October 2025.

While the Xbox Ally X is an incredible little device, its relatively small display has been outclassed by the likes of the Lenovo Legion Go 2 and MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ — even though they're much more expensive. But Asus took the 20th anniversary of ROG to update the Xbox Ally X with an OLED display, and it takes the handheld to a completely new level.

With a better display and a new chassis comes a higher $1,299 price tag, but if you have the cash, that extra $300 is absolutely worth it.

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 – Hands-On Photos

The Xbox Ally X20 has a fancier looking chassis and a much nicer OLED display, but it's functionally the same handheld as the Ally X beneath the surface with no real difference in the specs. It's still rocking the AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme, along with 24GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. It shouldn't be too surprising that performance is largely the same, netting 42 fps in Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p High settings with FSR set to Quality compared to 43 fps from the Xbox Ally X with the same settings.

In 3DMark, the performance also lines up. The Xbox Ally X20 gets 598 points in the Steel Nomad test, compared to 602 points from the original Xbox Ally X, which is within the margin of error. In Time Spy, the X20 gets 4,030 points, compared to 4,016 points from last year's model — also virtually the same performance.

Of course, because OLED displays are slightly more efficient than your standard LCD screen, the Xbox Ally X20's battery fares a bit better than its predecessor. Starting from 100% battery, I played Cyberpunk 2077 until the X20 died, and it lasted 2 hours and 43 minutes with all stock settings. That makes it the longest lasting handheld I've tested, beating out the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+'s 2 hours and 14 minutes, and the Xbox Ally X's 2 hours and 34 minutes. You're only getting an extra 10 minutes of battery life, so it's not exactly groundbreaking, but it is an improvement.

If you already have the Xbox Ally X, it's not worth upgrading to the X20 based on specs alone. But the star of the show is the improved OLED display.

While I still love the original Xbox Ally X, the display has always been a problem for me. In a lot of games, especially as time has gone on, I've found myself needing to squint at the screen in dark scenes to make out what's happening. Likewise, in games like Monster Hunter Rise (which I've unfortunately found myself recently obssessed with), the original Ally X's screen isn't great at making the bright colors pop off the screen as well as an OLED display can.

For a long time, that led me to daily driving the Lenovo Legion Go 2, which has its own problems. I have pretty small hands, and there are times where I struggle to stretch my thumb to hit all of the buttons. Plus, with all the dials and buttons built into the Joy-Con-like controllers on the Legion Go 2, it's easy to accidentally hit something and trick the game into thinking you're playing with a keyboard and mouse, even for just a second. But because the screen is so good, I would just power through, and it's become one of the default ways I play games in bed, whether it's something that's running locally on the Legion Go 2 or streaming through Moonlight.

After spending a few days with the Xbox Ally X20, I've shoved the Legion Go 2 back into storage. The X20's screen is smaller, but it's much easier to hold for long periods of time, which completely equalizes it for me. Plus, the crystal-clear display makes it easier to see whatever's on the screen, so having less real estate there doesn't make much of a difference.

While the new OLED display is the highlight, the Xbox Ally X20 also has a new, partially transparent chassis that's evocative of '90s gadget design. It does look great, even if I prefer the simple black aesthetic of the original. The menu buttons are all gold now, which is apparently the standard color of 'anniversary' or 'celebration' editions of tech products, and other buttons, like the volume rocker and all the standard controller inputs, are black.

What's more interesting is the D-pad. Asus worked in a transforming D-pad that you can pull out and rotate to transform it from a classically defined pad with four directional buttons to a concave version akin to what you'd find on the Xbox Elite controllers. A lot of controller makers do offer this choice, but it's usually handled by having a removable D-pad rather than one that can transform. If you do have a preference for one type of pad, you can set it that way, but really, I've just been fidgeting with it because of the satisfying clicking noise it makes whenever you pull it out and rotate it.

The sticks have also been updated from the standard sticks on the Xbox Ally X to new TMR sensors on the X20. Day to day, that difference hasn't been noticeable for me, but it does mean that they should last much longer without stick drift. That's super important in a device where, if the controller breaks, you can't easily swap out the controller or its parts without taking the whole thing apart.

Unfortunately, It's Still Running Windows

Just like any other handheld, what really holds the Xbox Ally X20 back from greatness is the software. Windows 11 is still a pain to use with a controller, and while the Xbox Full Screen Experience does mitigate many of the problems, there are still some definite issues.

In the few days I've spent with the Xbox Ally X20, I've run into one specific problem over and over again: If I try to swipe up on the display to go to another window, the controller will bug out. It acts as though the Xbox button is being held down, which means every button press is read as a shortcut, either opening the keyboard, pulling up the task manager, or some other silly behavior. It's bad enough when I'm trying to scroll through my library, but when I'm trying to pull up a guide in a browser and swap back and forth, it makes the X20 unusable until I reboot the thing.

To be fair, the original Xbox Ally X had problems with the Full Screen Experience when it launched, too. But that was when it was brand new, and none of the problems were as toxic to the experience as making the controller essentially non-functional. I've been able to get around these problems with the X20's UI by avoiding using the touchscreen as much as possible, but that's not something I should have to do with a $1,300 device, especially when it's essentially just a chassis and display upgrade.

This should be something that future updates should be able to fix, but in the meantime, I'd advise forgoing Windows and installing SteamOS or Bazzite, unless you really want to use it to play Game Pass games or Call of Duty.

Looking at what is essentially a PC version of the Nintendo Switch 2 and seeing a $1,299 price tag is going to turn some people off from the jump, but I'm still surprised that this handheld is as affordable as it is. The Xbox Ally X20 has nearly the same specs as the Lenovo Legion Go 2, except with 8GB less of RAM, but it costs $700 less at the time of writing.

It's not hard to look at other PC gaming hardware this year and imagine that Asus could have raised the price more, considering the much-improved display and the addition of TMR joysticks. Just look at the Steam Machine , which came in at $1,049, or even the 4-year-old Steam Deck , which Valve bumped up to $789 back in May. Compared to the Xbox Ally X20's Z2 Extreme, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD, the Steam Deck's aging RDNA 2 GPU, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB SSD at nearly $800 doesn't seem like that great of a deal at all.

Crucially, Asus also isn't discontinuing the existing Xbox Ally X, which is still a $999 handheld despite the price increases that have hit pretty much every other tech product this year. I keep bracing myself for what feels like the inevitability that Asus is going to raise its prices, but that hasn't happened yet. Now Asus is launching a new version of the Xbox Ally X, but with an OLED panel and TMR sticks for $1,299. That upgrade could be a bit cheaper, but it's hard to think of a single handheld gaming PC with an OLED display that is a better value right now.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Update 1.1 Adds Directional Animal Petting and Over 1,100 Other Improvements and Fixes
articles.summary: The Blood of Dawnwalker update 1.1 adds directional animal petting and over 1,100 other improvements and fixes.
articles.body:
Rebel Wolves really put out something special with The Blood of Dawnwalker , its vampire RPG where you straddle the line between monster and man. Now it’s getting even better with directional animal petting. Yeah, you heard.

Similar to Kingdom Come: Deliverance, Dawnwalker’s combat uses directional inputs to attack and defend from different angles during combat. Update 1.1, due out next week, will let you take that system and use it to frantically rub a dog.

“What happens when you merge a directional combat system with the ability to pet dogs and cats?” the studio asked . “Directional. Animal. Petting.”

The update also adds a consumable item: the Draught of Mind Rebirth. Take a sip and you’ll be able to respec all your upgrade points and try out a different build without starting the game again.

Elsewhere, the game is also getting an even easier mode for those who couldn’t get to grips with directional combat, as well as options for larger font sizes for the subtitles. Accessibility is always good.

There are also some visual upgrades coming, such as frame generation improvements, better animations and camera movement, improved lock-on and targeting, and better traversal. The Japanese version of the game has had all the blood and gore put back in, which is kinda vital for a game about a clan of human-sized leeches.

Rebel Wolves said there are over 1,100 other improvements in The Blood of Dawnwalker’ update 1.1. That’s a lot, and suggests a certain level of dedication. It shouldn't be a huge surprise though — the former The Witcher developers see the game as a starting point for an epic RPG series.

The Dawnwalker team has already teased where that future might take the series one day, with a CGI trailer depicting lead character Coen in the present day . The advantages of being an immortal halfbreed, eh? The Blood of Dawnwalker passed 1 million copies sold in its first two days, which suggests the team will at least get another game out. Whether that takes Coen straight to the present day or flips forward to another historical pinch point like Assassin’s Creed remains to be seen.

Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

articles.title: 7 Things We Learned Visiting the Set of Street Fighter
articles.summary: We visited the set of Street Fighter and discovered plenty about how a gigantic ensemble action movie comes together.
articles.body:
Towards the end of 2025, IGN was invited to the Sydney set of the new Street Fighter film, where we were able to spend a day wandering the sets and meeting the cast and crew of this nose-breaking, nunchuk-slinging dose of hard-hitting ’90s nostalgia.

Chaperoned by Noah Centineo, who plays Ken Masters, we met with stars Callina Liang and David Dastmalchian, stunt coordinator Jon Valera, and director Kitao Sakurai as they finalised filming on their bone-busting blockbuster.

Here’s everything we learned visiting the set of Street Fighter.

Yes, Callina Liang saw the concerns that she wouldn’t be able to bring Chun-Li’s legendary legs to life on screen. No, she doesn’t agree – and nor would her grandma, for that matter.

“I literally grew up playing the game, so as soon as my managers told me about the project I was, like, so excited,” says Liang. “Chun-Li was also the character I played, growing up.”

“I always had kind of thicker legs; I know the internet is, like, ‘Oh, her legs are not big enough!’ But, I don’t know, for some reason growing up I was always made fun of and my grandma would always be, like, ‘Oh hey, you got little fat legs!’ And playing with Chun-Li was the reason I stopped feeling insecure about them, so it just really feels like a dream come true, getting this role.”

There you have it, internet. You can’t disagree with grandma because, frankly, it’d be disrespectful.

2: Street Fighter’s Connection to Greek Mythology

Director Kitao Sakurai has a respect for Capcom’s cast of high-kicking characters as their own pantheon of modern day mythological heroes.

“To me it sort of feels a bit like Greek mythology, you know?” says Sakurai. “You have these characters that you have always known, and have always been part of the culture. Even if you never really grew up playing the game, and I wasn’t a huge gamer growing up; we never had a gaming system or anything like that. I would always go over to my friend’s house to play. But it was just infused into the culture, and these characters are just such an iconic part of culture in the world, that you can’t help but to think of them in terms of, ‘Oh, yeah, Ryu, and Ken, and Blanka.’ They’re so iconic and engraved into what we know of that time.”

Sakurai may not be the biggest gamer on set, but he does know a little about beating up gods on screen; that is, prior to his directorial career he did attack God with a hockey stick in 1999’s Dogma.

As a video game adaptation, Street Fighter may sit on the non-Shakespeare side of the storytelling spectrum, but Bison star David Dastmalchian is impressed with how seriously the huge cast is taking it – especially considering the mixed level of acting experience across the whole ensemble.

“I’ve been so impressed and grateful for the level of commitment that you see from 50 Cent showing up every day to go to the gym to train as a boxer, to Orville’s incredible work, to Callina, Rayna, and Mel and all of these performers that I’m around watching and seeing,” says Dastmalchian. “You know, Cody and Roman, professional athletes, who of course know about entertaining and they understand how to work with storytelling, but their commitment! Every single person. I’m sure I’m leaving a lot of people off of that list, but I swear to God, every single person who’s shown up that I’ve gotten a chance to either watch work, or work with, has taken this seriously the way I do and that made me feel really grateful.”

We’ve seen some very familiar fighting in the trailers already, but second unit director and stunt coordinator Jon Valera confirms the moves you know and love are here – and the actors themselves are the ones getting them done.

“We try and stay true to the game, try and bring the actual iconic moves to life,” says Valera. “We always want to please the fans and everybody out there, and it’s been great. We haven’t needed any digi-doubles or anything; all the guys are doing the iconic moves from the game.”

It’s new territory for Ken star Noah Centineo, but it’s a challenge he seems to have enjoyed.

“Yeah, it’s completely different; I’ve never done a film with martial arts, that’s for sure,” says Centineo. “I’ve never done a film with so much action. I’ve never done so many of the stunts myself.”

“We were here training for six weeks before we ever said, ‘Action!’ and working with Jon Velera, our stunt coordinator, under his guidance, and his team’s guidance. Yeah, it was an incredible process. We’re shooting main unit but also second unit simultaneously; second unit’s mainly a lot of the stunts and stuff. Being able to really fight and get into it. Or dance. It’s more like dancing; it’s choreographed dancing that looks like fighting; it’s awesome.”

5: Ken’s Favourite Characters are Blanka and Dhalsim

Like Chun-Li star Callina Liang, Ken star Noah Centineo also maintains fond memories of playing Street Fighter II in his early childhood. Unlike Liang, however, his favourite characters aren’t actually the one he’s playing in the film.

“My first interaction with Street Fighter, I must have been seven years old, or six years old, and my cousins that, at the time, lived in New Jersey – I went over to their house and in their basement they had one of the cabinet, old school arcade games of Street Fighter II. And I played that game religiously whenever I would make it up to New Jersey, which was, like, once a year for a lot of my early childhood. It was just countless hours spent playing that video game; playing Street FIghter II. I’d always play as Blanka, or Dhalsim. Those were my two favourite characters; I just thought they were sick.”

6: David Dastmalchian Might Have the Hardest Job Here

The original 1994 Street Fighter adaptation – starring Jean-Claude Van Damme, Raul Julia, and Ming-Na Wen, and coincidentally enough also filmed in Australia – was admittedly a strong commercial success. However, while it’s not a famously esteemed movie, there is one element of it held in enormous regard, and that’s Raul Julia’s impeccable performance as Bison. It was his final film appearance, with Julia passing away in the lead up to its release. New Bison star David Dastmalchian is conscious of the gravity added to the Bison role, with it being the most revered component of the 1994 film.

“So, with Bison, knowing how big of an impact Raul’s performance had on me and millions of other people, I wanted to carry a sense of honour for that, and honour it by doing the best job I can do,” he says. “And also let go and know that he would want me to bring David into the role, which is what Kitao asked me to do, which is the best thing I can ever do for something, and if I fail, I fail.”

“But I’ve got to bring all of David that I can, and also I’m trying my very best to honour a game that has such a special place in so many people’s hearts. So, when they watch, I pray that whatever I can bring out of me when they’re watching it, they forget about David. They maybe even forget about Raul for a minute, and they just see Bison. That is my dream. I guess we’ll see.”

“My son is the biggest gamer I know. Both of my kids – my son and my daughter – are so excited about seeing me do this, and they’re very, very honest critics. So they’re gonna see this movie and, as soon as they walk out, they’re gonna either turn to me and go, ‘Good job, Dad’ or they’re gonna go, ‘ Eh, sus.’ So I’m praying for [the former].”

7: If Fans of the Game Like It, That’s a Victory

So what will represent a win for Centineo?

“I hope that people see it, and the people that have grown up playing the game, and still play the game and love the game and live by the game, watch the movie and go, ‘Yeah, they did the game justice,’ says Centineo. “I think that’s the biggest thing for me; those that have played the game, and grew up playing the game and know the game well, watch the movie and go, ‘Yeah, they respected the game; they respected our world, and we appreciate that.”

“And I hope that people that aren’t too familiar with the game watch the movie and walk away going, ‘Yeah, that a great movie and it was a cool world, and I wanna see more of that.’”

Street Fighter is in cinemas this week. IGN’s review of the film says there’s an “infectious and celebratory energy coursing through Kitao Sakurai’s Street Fighter at every turn,” even if it “never lets good sense get in the way of a good time.”

Luke Reilly is an award-winning journalist with 23 years of media experience across Official PlayStation Magazine, Australian 360, and IGN – which he joined in 2011. You can find him on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
articles.summary: Three Verge writers spent the week testing five configurations of Windows laptops from Microsoft, Asus, HP, and Lenovo — each with Nvidia’s new RTX Spark N1X “superchip.”
articles.body: Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models. The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own Tom Warren fully reviewed. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing. All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a Surface Laptop Ultra or a smaller Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM. These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s a lot to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week. Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep? Does it just work? [Image: A laptop costing $7,000 better just work, and work well. Antonio Di Benedetto: Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer. Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities. Sean Hollister: Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode. But I largely agree with Antonio. I made an RTX Spark my daily driver, with all my typical work and personal apps — Signal, Discord, Audacity, CapCut and Evernote, Irfanview, Slack, ScreenToGif and more — and nothing has failed me so far. I never once needed to think whether I was running an Arm or an x86 app. The real hitches came with gaming and AI, as you’ll read below. Tom Warren: I’ve been using a Windows on Arm laptop with a Qualcomm chip daily for the past two years and things have improved to the point that I can’t tell if an app is native or not anymore. That’s the same story on the RTX Spark laptops, and I feel like Nvidia’s entry into this category will only improve the story for creative apps and gaming. Can it game? [Image: Gears of War: E-Day running on the Surface Laptop Ultra during a Microsoft demo. TW: Windows on Arm never looked like a serious gaming platform before now. While there still aren’t many native Arm games, Nvidia’s GPU helps bruteforce through the emulation layer. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games. I mostly game on my desktop, where I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps. In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go. SH: Like Tom says, the GPU power is there — but the CPU might hold back some of your games. I had plenty of power for a smooth 60fps in Returnal (at 1440p with high settings), Expedition 33 (at a DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with high settings), Jedi Survivor (DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with medium settings), and Shadow of the Tomb Raider (at native 1800p and highest spec). But when I fired up Helldivers 2, even dipping down to a DLSS-upscaled 1080p was no guarantee of 60fps in the highest difficulty missions. There are just too many enemies on screen for the Spark to keep up. Star Wars Zero Company is even more CPU-bound — the Spark didn’t care whether I was maximizing or minimizing the graphics and screen resolution. No matter what I tried, I typically saw my framerate capped between 37fps and 39fps in battle. Even ancient and low-powered games can have quirks. I tried the 2003 title Max Payne 2 and saw situations where framerate dipped to 50fps. I even saw a few hitches in the excellent UFO 50, a collection of 2D games, though a couple other 2D games ran great. I’m also not sure if RTX Spark is suitable for VR yet. The excellent Titanfall 2 VR mod worked, and it seemed to run fine at first, but lost a little stability after a few minutes. That could be my Wi-Fi, because the driver for Valve’s Steam Frame wireless adapter wouldn’t install on the Spark. Neither did Steam’s streaming audio solution, so the audio came out of the Nvidia laptop instead of the headset. Just so we’re clear, all of this is assuming you want a laptop maxing out its fans and positively dumping heat on your desk or lap. That’s not unusual for thin gaming notebooks, but it’s way louder and hotter than a good desktop or handheld. AD: I’ve wanted a MacBook Pro-like laptop with full PC gaming chops for as long as I can remember, so I was hyped for these laptops to deliver the goods in graphics. The first night, I set up the Asus ProArt P16, with all 128GB of its ridiculously large pool of memory, and when I booted up Big Walk for my planned online evening with some friends my first thought was, “Well, that looks okay. I guess.” I know Big Walk isn’t some triple-A graphical titan, but it has some fairly demanding graphics for the “friend slop” genre. I expected the N1X to max it out, or at least get close, but not really. I had to bump the P16’s 4K display down to 2560 x 1600, and instead of Big Walk’s Highest or Very high graphics presets, I brought it down to High to maintain a decently solid 60-ish fps. Does any of that really matter for this silly co-op game about solving puzzles with your buddies? Of course not. It looked fine, after all. But it was a sobering reminder that this “superchip” is no graphical magician. As Tom and Sean point out, RTX Spark can do some decent gaming, but temper your expectations for medium or even low settings in some cases, and be ready to rely on DLSS and frame gen. There’s no denying that cheaper desktops and even laptops with discrete Nvidia graphics cards can easily beat out an N1X. Nvidia claims it’s like having an RTX 5070 Laptop GPU in an SoC, but in my testing it was somewhere between that and an RTX 5060 Laptop GPU — not a slouch, for sure, but if you’re a gamer first your money goes much further with traditional Nvidia graphics cards. How’s the battery life? [Image: Sadly, only Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra has that slick magnetic USB-C charging. SH: Nvidia’s partners saw fit to equip their first wave of RTX Spark laptops with some of the biggest batteries you can bring on an airplane with no questions asked — but even with a 99.9 watt-hour pack like the one in my Asus ProArt P16, these laptops won’t be winning awards for longevity. While Tom and Antonio spent their days testing every use case under the sun, I made the P16 my daily driver for normal work while watching the battery meter like a hawk. That mostly means writing stories in a web browser, and it’s not quite lasting the day. My best run was 5 hours and 40 minutes of real-world work at 50 percent brightness, including an hour-long video call with Tom and Antonio to strategize our RTX Spark coverage plan. The next day, I got only about 5 hours from a full charge because I spent two of them editing this video in Capcut. The third time I drained the battery, it took 5 hours, too. With web work, I’m typically seeing 13-17 watt battery drain on the laptop’s default settings, but that climbs to 20-30 watts with light video work, up to 50 watts during the (brief) Capcut video export, and I made it jump all the way to 120 watts playing Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. The battery couldn’t keep feeding at that rate — it slowly went down, and at 30 percent charge I saw a big performance hit as it dropped dramatically to 60 watts. The good news is the Asus charges fast from a 140W USB-C PD power source. It took 20 minutes to go from dead to 50 percent battery, another 15 minutes to get to 70 percent, and a total of 1 hour, 15 minutes to reach 95 percent charge. AD: I’ve had to run lots of benchmarks while plugged in, so I haven’t been able to spend as much time testing battery life as I’d normally like. Anecdotally, in lots of fits and starts, battery life seems solid. As Sean saw, you’re unlikely to get through a full eight hour work day unless you’re going out of your way to be efficient. And if you fire up anything heavy, like a local AI model (more on that in a minute), you won’t even make it to lunch. I’ll eventually do more thorough battery testing as I continue using these laptops, including our usual rundown tests for a bit of 1:1 comparisons. Does local AI seem useful? [Image: A local AI model running on a Surface Laptop Ultra. TW: Not yet. It all feels like a beta aimed at developers right now: from the install experience of AI agents flashing up command prompts and Visual Studio, to the fans blasting away for the most basic of queries. I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, running tasks that developers would favor. It’s also nice to have this all on a local device, without having to share emails and files with a cloud service and worry about the privacy aspects. Still, I would regularly close OpenClaw or Hermes and not let them run in the background all day, especially if I had given them permissions to access local files. I’m just not ready to trust AI fully, local or not. Microsoft and Nvidia both envision a future where AI agents automate things on your PC, but I’m still not fully convinced. While there are some mundane tasks I could certainly automate, I like using my PC to edit photos or videos, write, and play games. I don’t want to sit there and watch a robot do all of that for me. That’s part of the joy of computing to me. SH: I walked out of Nvidia’s Editor’s Day thinking I might finally have a reason to fire up local AI. I asked Hermes, running Qwen3.8-27B, to build me a daily news briefing much like the one in Nvidia’s on-stage demo. It took 10 minutes, and 10 percent of my entire 99.9 watt-hour battery, to finally produce a list of stories that took the cloud-based Claude (Opus 5.5) half as long — while utterly monopolizing my GPU and dramatically heating up the Spark laptop. The laptop stayed hot and a little sluggish as long as I kept Hermes open. Claude also produced better results, with more detail and better sourcing. I guess I got the local AI tokens for “free,” I wouldn’t trust Claude with my email, and I probably could have used a smaller, lighter model. But I went with what the program recommended, and that was the result. I tried a clean reinstall of Hermes to make sure it wasn’t a misconfiguration, but this time, the prompt took even longer and used 60 percent of my battery. Ouch. [Image: [Image: AD: I’m still early in my journey of learning to use local AI, and these RTX Spark laptops are obviously a viable — albeit, expensive — option. But even if you have 128GB of memory to use some chunky models, it’s still not a user-friendly experience for beginners. Microsoft’s Get Started intro in Windows 11 gives you easy one-click installs for Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. (Which all have ESRB ratings for some reason?) But after that, you’re kind of on your own. I stuck with Hermes, since that’s what I was already using on the Mac Studio, but if you’re using it on a system with 32GB of RAM or less it just tells you there isn’t enough memory for its recommended local Qwen models — either routing you towards the cloud or fully relying on you to go fetch a smaller model on your own. Using local AI has major privacy advantages over cloud models, but it’s definitely less convenient since local LLMs are much slower to process and more taxing on your system. Churning a local model through your laptop’s memory tears through any of these laptops’ large batteries, and the results from LLMs are still mixed. I burned through 30 percent of the Lenovo Yoga 9n’s battery in 36 minutes to get a Qwen 3.8 27B model to resize and add a white background to five product images in PNG format — and it cropped the images wrong and cut off the products. I got it to do it right after a couple follow-up prompts, and grabbing the power cable to prevent Hermes from killing the laptop in the process. Is the hardware truly great? [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: AD: These laptops are very expensive, but that also means the manufacturers are mostly bringing their A-games. Across the Asus, HP, Lenovo, and what I gathered from Tom’s thoughts on the Surface, the RTX Spark line is awash in great-to-excellent haptic trackpads, keyboards, screens, and speakers. The metal builds of the three I’m testing feel great to the touch. The OLED displays all look fantastic. And each of these are decently thin for the kind of workstation-class laptops that they are. If I had to pick one for myself based on hardware alone I’d probably choose the Asus ProArt. It ticks the most boxes for me with its three USB-C ports, super bright display, superior inverted-T arrow cluster, and full SD card slot. The HP actually feels the nicest, with an impressively rock-solid chassis, but at nearly five pounds it’s the heaviest of the bunch, and its microSD card slot is much less useful to me. As for the Lenovo, it’s actually been my sleeper favorite. It’s the only 2-in-1 in this crop I’ve been testing, and that just makes it more flexible (pun intended) and fun. You can use its large stylus on either the screen or the large trackpad, giving it lots more potential for graphics and design work. And tent mode with a large 16-inch 120Hz OLED is a delight for the occasional gaming session or watching shows and movies — it’s just not as bright as the Asus. SH: I’ve only truly driven the Asus P16 so far, but I was impressed with the build quality of the whole spectrum of RTX Spark launch laptops at Nvidia’s Editor’s Day. The Asus P16 probably wouldn’t be my pick personally because of its extra glossy screen and oversensitive touchpad. I like to use my laptops in rooms with lots of ambient light, and find I have to crank up the brightness of this machine’s otherwise excellent calibrated OLED screen. Meanwhile, my palms keep tapping my mouse cursor on things I didn’t mean to tap, just because they accidentally brush the touchpad while typing. The speakers and webcam also leave something to be desired, but the Windows Hello face login and proximity sensing are excellent. As soon as I walk away, the screen dims, and I’m logged right back in just by looking at my laptop. Despite the heat, Asus’ fans aren’t shrill — they’re very loud and noticeable while gaming, but at least it’s whoosh rather than whine. TW: While I ran into some weird bugs with the Surface Laptop Ultra during testing, I can’t fault the hardware. The look and feel is very similar to a MacBook Pro, and the magnetic USB-C port really feels like something Apple should have done — it’s that good. The large haptic trackpad carries on the tradition of great Surface trackpads, with the added benefit of subtle haptic feedback when you move windows around or align objects in apps like PowerPoint. I would have preferred an OLED display on the Laptop Ultra, but I found switching away from the default “Vivid” color option to “Enhanced” improved the contrast on the mini-LED panel. I also really appreciate the port section on the Laptop Ultra, especially that there’s a full SD card reader and even a USB-A port. Check out my full review for more thoughts. Is it fast? Does it hang with Apple M-series chips? AD: Yes, the RTX Spark N1X is a powerful chip. These high-end laptop configurations we’ve been testing with lots of unified memory are meant to compete with the Pro and Max chips in Apple’s MacBook Pros. And while they can hang in some GPU performance tests, like tying the top spec M5 Max in a Blender render, Apple’s CPUs are much more powerful. Apple has put lots of development into its in-house processors and the extra-fast “super cores” of its M6, M5 Pro, and M5 Max chips. And, frankly, nothing competes with those chips in single core performance — not even Nvidia’s “superchip.” (Seriously, can we stop with the word super?) But the part that stings most about the RTX Spark’s 20-core CPU is that even a lowly 12-core M6 Mac Mini competes with it in multicore performance — and a Mac Mini starts at just $900. It’s awesome to see this kind of graphics performance without the need for a discrete GPU, allowing for thinner system designs with less noisy fans. I’m into it, just as I was with AMD’s Strix Halo APU — but like Strix Halo, Nvidia’s RTX Spark is a pricey part. And there’s no denying that Apple’s offerings are more well-rounded performers, so long as you don’t care as much about games. TW: It’s definitely up there, but I think Qualcomm comes closer to Apple’s M-series chips on the CPU side. Qualcomm also had years of experimentation with Windows on Arm before it acquired Nuvia and managed to create a competitive chip with the Snapdragon X series. I think Nvidia will need a similar amount of work to catch up on the CPU side for future RTX Spark chips. The development of the RTX Spark took at least three years, and I had heard from sources familiar with Nvidia’s plans that the chips were supposed to launch last year. So work has been ongoing, but the CPU side is still a little disappointing. Nvidia picked MediaTek for its Arm-based CPU, a chipmaker that is better known for the Wi-Fi hardware in laptops, not the CPUs. I sure hope the next-generation is more powerful. The whole time I’ve been testing the Surface Laptop Ultra I couldn’t help but think the forbidden dream would be a combination of a Qualcomm CPU and Nvidia GPU. I can’t see that ever happening in reality, but it would certainly be interesting to see. So what’s our take on RTX Spark so far? [Image: A chip this powerful in a 2-in-1 this large, with a stylus? Nifty. TW: I think it will elevate interest in Windows on Arm for creative and gaming tasks, simply because we haven’t had Arm-based Windows laptops that are really capable of running games until now. Nvidia is targeting creators and developers with its first round of RTX Spark laptops, but there’s definitely a gap here for a more affordable version focused on gaming. Perhaps that’s the N1 chips we’ve heard rumors about. SH: Nice, but too pricey. Too hot and loud when you’re doing the things that would theoretically justify that price. I care what they stand for, and the direction they’re pointed, far more than I care to own one. AD: I love that there is now even more competition in the laptop space, but the super high prices makes RTX Spark laptops mostly unattainable. I want to see lower cost options come around, as well as an eventual second generation with higher CPU performance to hopefully close the gap further with Apple. I also hope this helps push development for Arm-based and Arm-compatible games forward. Maybe it could even one day mean easier porting of games to macOS. Wouldn’t that be a fun outcome? As cool as it will be to keep testing these super high-end RTX Spark models, I’m most hyped to get my hands on a base Surface Laptop Ultra or Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM and see how they stack up to the entry-level 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro. That’s my personal sweet spot for Apple’s lineup — the people’s MacBook Pro. (Well, okay, less these days now that it starts at two-grand.) It’s an exciting time in computing when it comes to chip choice, but it’s also an absolutely cursed time thanks to RAMageddon and sky high prices. I’m constantly wondering what laptops like these RTX Sparks or even Googlebooks might have cost if AI demands didn’t drive up the prices of RAM and storage. I have no idea who is going to spend up to $7,000 on these laptops when PC sales as a whole seem on a downward trend, but it’s cool they exist.

articles.title: 'We F***ed Up' — Wardogs Boss Admits Season 2 Hasn't Gone Particularly Well
articles.summary: Wardogs developer Bulkhead had some strong words to say about the rough launch of Season 2, admitting: "We f***ed up."
articles.body:
Wardogs developer Bulkhead had some strong words to say about the rough launch of Season 2, admitting: "We f***ed up."

Season 2 saw the introduction of XP and cash bonuses for people willing to play Blue Team, in an attempt to polish Lonestar’s tarnished reputation .

Unfortunately, the idea backfired as more experienced players quickly boosted their accounts on Blue. Usually it takes a while for players to unlock some of the deadliest gear, but the XP and cash boosts saw players quickly kitted out in the best armor and the most annoying weapons.

"We were wrong, we f***ed up," Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer said. "This was an experiment — we thought we'd have this in for about a week.” The boosts have already been removed in a hotfix.

The cash and XP bonuses saw Blue Team go from the worst performing team to quickly dominating every match, attracting all the best players. The bonuses were 5% extra cash and 2.5% extra XP, but it was enough to attract the most try-hard players in the game.

"The only comment that annoyed me is when people say, 'They didn't address the core issues [with Blue Team]," Brammer continued, talking about team spawn placement. "Well, actually, we did rebalance the entire spawn setup for Bakurani, and we did test that out quite a lot and see that the difference had balanced out.

“We should have just stuck to our guns with that, really, but here we are — we tried, it didn't work, this is us holding our hands up."

Wardogs is still in Early Access so these kinds of teething issues are to be expected as the devs experiment and find the right balance for the 1.0 release. The game exploded in terms of sales, and the developers have been scrambling to keep up with its popularity since.

Bulkhead also had to contend with making sure Wardogs works on consoles, where the game will eventually land in 1.0. The developer already admitted to having to hold back Wardogs features to make sure it’ll run on Xbox Series S .

Wardogs Season 2 also introduced a new rain system that impacts gameplay. Players have to really cock their heads to pick up footsteps, and visibility for pilots is drastically reduced.

articles.title: Elon Musk's Tesla Flying Car Reveal Met With Mix of Astonishment and Skepticism
articles.summary: Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled a car that he claims can fly, followed by a short demonstration of its ability to go airborne — and it's hard to think of a Tesla vehicle that's sparked more online reaction since the Cybertruck.
articles.body:
Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled a car that he claims can fly, followed by a short demonstration of its ability to go airborne — and it's hard to think of a Tesla vehicle that's sparked more online reaction since the Cybertruck .

The demonstration was held outside of a Texas SpaceX test facility , where Musk unveiled the car in front of a live audience. During that demonstration, Musk took to the stage, where he said, "We need an audience to prove it's not AI or SI, so you guys can tell people you saw it with your eyes," and that, "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration between the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company."

When the flying Roadster was revealed, it was remotely piloted to "make sure we don't kill anyone." The demo started off with the car facing a steep ramp, where it used suction to drive and park upside down, before eventually zooming up the ramp, jumping off, using rockets to right itself and land safely.

Turns out the future does have flying cars — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 16, 2026

Turns out the future does have flying cars

The car uses thrusters from SpaceX in the rear of the vehicle and along the bottom to "basically fly like a rocket." Musk admitted this is "not necessarily a safety-optimized car," which is likely why, earlier in the event, he claimed that it would be "long-term the only manually driven car that Tesla makes." Musk added that this new Roadster would enter production in 2028, but with something like this, I'd expect a number of delays, if it ever makes it to the street at all.

Regardless, the car has been blowing people's minds. Christopher Lloyd, who famously played flying car driver Doc Brown in the Back to The Future movies, took to X / Twitter to say: "Finally...flying cars." Meanwhile, other folks, like user CARN0N tweeted out highlight reels of all the stunts that Tesla pulled off with the prototype rocket car. Some have even compared it to Rocket League.

Highlights of all four stunts Tesla showed off with the new Roadster today. — Oli (@CARN0N) October 16, 2026

Highlights of all four stunts Tesla showed off with the new Roadster today.

"Rocket League is just a video game" Tesla engineers: — Spawn Wave (@SpawnWaveMedia) October 16, 2026

"Rocket League is just a video game" Tesla engineers:

There is a healthy dose of skepticism, of course. Tech influencer MKBHD tweeted out his disbelief, saying, "They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4,000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028. This is a prank, right?"

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman was impressed, even if he was a bit skeptical, tweeting: "Hard to think of a wilder product unveiling. Not sure how quickly drivers are going to be leaping over each other in traffic, but damn, this was a cool way to introduce Roadster to the world."

Only time will tell if this new flying Roadster will ever actually see the light of day, or if it'll even be street legal in most places when it does. Musk sure seemed hopeful that Tesla would be able to get it out the door and into customer's hands in the next couple years, but really, we'll just have to wait and see.

Photo by FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images.

articles.title: Apparent Leaked Footage Shows Canceled Assassin's Creed Game Set in Qin Dynasty China
articles.summary: Ubisoft was apparently making another Assassin’s Creed game set in ancient China, except this one was a full-fat AC with a massive open world and a fancy umbrella weapon.
articles.body:
Ubisoft was apparently making another Assassin’s Creed game set in ancient China, except this one was a full-fat AC with a massive open world and a fancy umbrella weapon. According to a new report, the game was called Assassin’s Creed Destiny.

Assassin’s Creed Jade will explore the same setting, targeting mobile. Destiny’s prototype footage appears to be aimed at modern consoles and PC instead.

Destiny was reportedly set during 206 BCE, where the Qin dynasty made way for the Han dynasty after a brutal civil war. The game likely would have focused on Liu Bang’s rise to power.

MP1st found the footage in developer portfolios. According to the report, the game was supposed to be a partnership between Ubisoft and Tencent, the Chinese conglomerate that owns huge portions of the games industry, including a 25% stake in Vantage Studios, a subsidiary that oversees some of Ubisoft’s biggest IPs.

The footage shows a hooded assassin battling through a siege headed up by warlord Xiang Yu, before switching to greybox testing environments for combat abilities. There’s a spinning umbrella weapon shown at one point.

Another snippet suggests players would have been able to choose between a male and female character, or it could have done the Shadows thing of having dual protagonists. Yin-yangs and ink brushes are used to tie the UI into the setting thematically.

While Destiny was seemingly cancelled, Assassin’s Creed Jade is still in development. The last we heard about it was that it was delayed to 2025 . Considering it’s 2026 now, it’s probably safe to assume they’re having some issues getting the mobile game off the ground, which is ironic for a series about assassins who love rooftops.

Elsewhere in the world of hidden blades, leaps of faith, and stylish hoods, Assassin’s Creed Hexe is the next major game in the series. If leaks are to be believed, that’s got its own development issues, mind you. One report suggests Assassin’s Creed Hexe developers decided to rework the game, removing magical abilities from the mix.

Hexe's game director Benoit Richer recently departed the project for reasons unknown. That departure followed the exit of Clint Hocking, Hexe's creative director , sparking the beginning of a major internal reshuffle at the top of the franchise that saw Ubisoft veteran Jean Guesdon ascend to become Assassin's Creed Head of Content.

articles.title: VisionQuest Fans Think the MCU Show Is Hiding a Major Character Right Under Their Noses
articles.summary: VisionQuest watchers believe they've spotted another major MCU character in the new show's first episode.
articles.body:
VisionQuest watchers believe they've spotted another major MCU character in the new show's first episode.

Paul Bettany reappeared as The Vision when his standalone Disney+ series premiered its first two episodes earlier this week. Although familiar Tony Stark-created AI bots like Jarvis (James D'Arcy), Edith (Emily Hampshire), and even Ultron (James Spader) are already keeping the hero company within his troubled mind, some fans believe VisionQuest has snuck in another big name from the WandaVision trilogy.

Warning! Potential spoilers for VisionQuest follow.

That character is none other than Wanda and Vision's magic-wielding son, Billy Maximoff, a.k.a. Wiccan. Played by Heartstopper actor Joe Locke in the 2024 Marvel show Agatha All Along , eagle-eyed viewers believe the character made his first appearance in the closing moments of the Vision show's first episode. If it really is him and it slipped by you, don't beat yourself up too hard; this is more of a blink-and-you'll-miss-it Easter Egg than an outright reveal.

After VisionQuest sets up White Vision's struggle with his identity, the first episode spends some time introducing another new face for a character we've already met. Wanda and Vision's other child, Tommy, seems to be alive after possessing the body of another human being (played by Ruaridh Mollica). Instead of materializing just outside of Westview like his brother, Billy, though, Tommy is living life in London as a pickpocket.

If fan suspicions are to be believed, Billy is well aware of his brother's location. After Tommy pulls off a small heist toward the end of Episode 1, one person with a familiar haircut can be seen walking amongst the crowd. Then, when Tommy meets up with his accomplice, Lisa (Lauren Morais), later down the road, that same person can be seen again, but this time, they're in a completely different position.

Could it be an extra out of place or a minor continuity error, or is it actually our first look at Wiccan's return as the WandaVision trilogy comes to an end? That's what fans are trying to figure out, but considering the MCU is known for tucking away the occasional visual Easter Egg and trick, many viewers wouldn't be surprised if this is our first hint at a family reunion.

The streets are saying Billy is following Tommy around… Oh, WandaVision-level delusions. WE ARE SO BACK! #VisionQuest — alias (@itsjustanx) October 15, 2026

The streets are saying Billy is following Tommy around… Oh, WandaVision-level delusions. WE ARE SO BACK! #VisionQuest

Wiccan's return is something fans have expected in the weeks leading up to VisionQuest's premiere. Aside from the fact that the show, which happens to be the last before Avengers: Doomsday marks the beginning of the end of the Multiverse Saga this December, offers an opportunity to reunite a powerful Marvel family, one recent trailer may also have contained another hint at Wiccan's return . The most damning evidence of his role in the show, however, is the fact that Mollica kind of let it slip that he and Locke had filmed some scenes together during an interview with Entertainment Tonight .

"It was amazing," Tommy's actor said of working with Locke on VisionQuest. "We actually shot our MCU stuff before we did the play [Clarkston], which was amazing. We met for a coffee beforehand to get to know each other, and we were just so excited. We became such good friends instantly, and then we did a play on the West End together and had this big secret that slowly started to leak as we were doing it."

Well, it all seems to be out there now, but we'll have to wait to see if the mysterious figure shown in Episode 1 really was Wiccan undercover. Until then, VisionQuest episodes will continue to roll out weekly . We'll get two episodes every week until the penultimate episode arrives November 3. The finale, Episode 8: "Forever," will then drop November 10.

For those who have yet to start VisionQuest, be sure to catch up on everything you need to know here . You can also see why Bettany thinks his Vision feels abandoned by the Avengers .

articles.title: Get a Switch 2-Ready 512GB MicroSD Express Card for $85
articles.summary: This microSD Express card deal lets you expand your Switch 2 storage for as cheap as you'll find in 2026.
articles.body:
If you have a Nintendo Switch 2, there’s a good chance you’re running low on storage. That’s because it only comes with 256GB. And with more people buying digital games than ever before, that amount can fill up fast. Thankfully, Walmart is selling a Switch 2-ready 512GB microSD Express card for $84.77 — way less than you’ll pay for that much storage elsewhere (for reference, Amazon has a SanDisk one for $129.99). This card is almost never in stock, so grab it while it's available.

Onn is Walmart’s in-house brand, and this card has a great customer rating, and our review calls it, and I quote, "fine." Since microSD Express cards have no moving parts, they’re generally quite reliable – I’ve never had any trouble with one. All you have to do is put it in your Switch 2, format it as a storage device, and you can start downloading games from the eShop onto it immediately.

In prior years, the price of storage would reliably go down as time marched on, but then AI came along and AI companies started buying up most of the world’s supply of storage for data centers, and RAMageddon or whatever you want to call it began. Storage prices have been going up since late last year, and it doesn’t look like they’ll be coming down anytime soon, if ever.

Which is a huge bummer, because in the 4K era, games take up more storage than ever before. For instance, the Switch 2 version of Final Fantasy VII Rebirth takes up nearly 100GB of storage, which is nearly half of what comes on Nintendo’s console. Other AAA game take up a big chunk, too, like Assassin’s Creed Shadows (62GB), Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition (60GB), and Madden NFL 27 (57GB).

All of which is to say, you’ll probably want more storage on your Switch 2 unless you enjoy juggling game installs on and off the device. And you’re not going to find a better price on microSD Express cards right now. This thing effectively triples the amount of storage on a Switch 2, which gives you much more breathing room.
