articles.title: ‘It Was an Unofficial Goal of the Team to Be Banned, Unrated, or Restricted’ – How Hellraiser: Revival Expands Cenobite Lore While Staying True to Clive Barker
articles.summary: Hellraiser: Revival understands Clive Barker on a much deeper level than just gore and sex — it's a deeply authentic extension of the horror master's Cenobite universe.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains spoilers for Hellraiser: Revival.

The first five minutes of Hellraiser: Revival will make your eyebrows high-five the ceiling. It opens with a BDSM-flavored sex scene complete with piercing and blood and a veritable buffet of sex toys scattered around the room, then evolves into a gory example of what hooks and chains can do to flesh. If you're sweet and innocent you might want to clutch some pearls, but to Clive Barker fans like me it's a signal that Revival is committing to the spirit of the author and director’s sexy subversion rather than watering it down. And I'm not an easy woman to please. The original Hellraiser movie rewired my brain when I saw it as a teenager (yes, I have a therapist), and Barker's Books of Blood volumes are in my top five reads of all time. I was bracing for disappointment, but that opening proved that Revival wasn't going to shy away from the body horror or sex that runs through Barker's work. The Hellraiser world is one of horrible and hedonistic extremes, so trying to avoid either would be like trying to swap Beyond Meat patties for prime rib. And the deeper I got into Hellraiser: Revival, the clearer it became that the game's understanding of those extremes went beyond pure sex and gore.

Expanding on any existing fiction, especially one as iconic as the Hellraiser series, is a challenge for anyone. Luckily, developer Saber Interactive was able to work with its creator directly, with Nenad Tomic, Revival’s executive producer, telling Xbox Wire that Barker was "deeply involved with the game from the very beginning" and shaped everything from "visual style and story motifs to the lore and character personalities." From a player experience perspective, it's key that the game stars the OG Pinhead, Doug Bradley, because no one wants a bad impersonator ruining the party.

Some parallels are obvious. Saber Interactive has explicitly said that Revival’s protagonist, Aidan, was inspired by Julia from Barker’s novella The Hellbound Heart and its film adaptation, Hellraiser, and you can see the game playing with the same themes of obsessive attachment, sexual need, and total simp behavior. Julia is willing to act as a honey trap to secure victims for her oozing lover, while Aidan is ready to make a deal with Pinhead and then go on a killing spree to bring back his girl. It's at once beautiful and twisted, and if nothing else a step up from a man who rolls his eyes when you ask him to share his fries. Never settle, ladies.

"Like Julia, Aidan is a character experiencing a fundamental dissatisfaction with life,” Antony De Fault, Hellraiser: Revival’s narrative director, tells me. “His heart yearns for feelings of purpose and vitality, and like Julia, the object of that fixation is a person with an even deeper dissatisfaction, who accelerates his self-destructive tendencies. In Aidan’s case, that’s his girlfriend Sunny.

"The most significant difference between the two is that Julia has suppressed her yearning for a long time, attempting to play the ‘good housewife,' whereas Aidan has pursued it,” De Fault continues. “This history of troublemaking and criminality makes him more worldly, and in particular, more equipped for violence.

"This was a deliberate departure from Julia’s mold, since Aidan is a player character in an FPS horror game. We wanted to give the player a variety of gameplay experiences, which included stealth, exploration, and enemies you can’t directly fight (the experiences of Kirsty in the movies), but also ‘game-y’ experiences like combat challenges and resource management. For those, a more competent character like Aidan made sense."

Throughout Hellraiser: Revival’s story, we get to see flashbacks of Sunny and Aidan’s relationship and better understand how a devotion strong enough to send you into the Labyrinth, the Cenobites’ hellish dimension ruled by Leviathan, develops. The ties that bind you need to be stronger than meeting at a work Christmas party and sharing a love of Netflix reality shows for that sort of errand. Aidan was a drug addict, now Sunny is his fix – she changed his life and he's not sure what trying to go on without her would even look like. We also get a little glimpse at what happens when only one half of a couple is on board with worshipping at the altar of pleasure and pain thanks to a couple called Sean and Charlotte, whose story we learn through letters scattered around the world. Spoiler: It is not a happy ending.

As well as ensuring fans get to see all their favorites – Pinhead, Butterball, and my personal nightmare fuel, Chatterer – Hellraiser: Revival makes its own contribution to the lore by diving deeper into the idea of an organized religion, The Scarlet Church, developing around the Cenobites. The films have played with the idea before (check out Hellraiser: Deader), but Revival goes all in on a doctrine, some seriously intense interior decor choices, and a brutal path to ascension. In its teachings, pain is a gift that can be given and received, and even a kindness, though it's not beyond exploiting people when it comes to recruiting new members.

"In a practical sense, we knew that the player couldn’t fight the Cenobites, and that simply running away from them wasn’t going to support an entire game,” explains De Fault. “So we had good cause to invent some sort of force that would often oppose the player in their stead, while still evoking the Cenobites and feeling like it belonged in the world of Hellraiser.

"From there, the leap to a Cenobite-inspired cult seems pretty logical, especially given the religious themes present in Clive’s work," he says.

The church's congregation is the mutilated faithful, whose hobbies include sticking knives in people and wearing latex. De Fault explains that, like the parallels between Aidan and Julia, the church in some ways represents Frank from the original Hellraiser.

"They’re people who are so dissatisfied with life, so numb to it, that they will go to incredible extremes in their pursuit of intense experiences that make them feel vital,” he says.

"But like Frank, as you’ll discover in the game, the Scarlet Church aren’t actually prepared for the reality of what the Cenobites offer. They seek the Cenobites because they want hedonic pleasure, or power, as opposed to what the Cenobites really are, which is more spiritual (“Explorers, in the further regions of experience”). The only one who really ‘gets it’ is their misunderstood Prophet, Bruno."

Another key player in the cult is an unhinged doctor called Colin Marlowe, who shares an approach to elective surgery that would make even Beverly Hills trophy wives think, "Now steady on." And then there's Charlotte, who gives an insight into why someone might follow the teachings of the church, writing things like, "There is divinity in my wretchedness, splendor in every ugly part of me," and "For the first time in my life, I feel accepted and understood. I can be myself... my true self... the Scarlet Church gave me that truth.” For her, submitting to the church represents acceptance, identity, and a way to see the parts of herself she despises as sacred rather than shameful.

"Without wanting to trigger any lawyering, we looked at real cults and cult-like organizations,” reveals De Fault. “I think that most people who fall prey to these systems do so because they are desperate for belonging, liberation, or to think they’re ‘one of the good people.'

"And in a way, the Scarlet Church does offer those things. There’s an extreme acceptance and intimacy and the promise that they will enlighten others (including by force) to share those ‘gifts’ with them. These ‘attraction’ elements are primarily conveyed to the player through the voices and writing of cult members themselves."

While the cult members tend to run around trying to kill you and promising to jerk you off once you're dead, the environmental storytelling, documents, and audio recordings (horror games are single-handedly keeping the dictaphone trade alive, it seems) help reveal more about the motives different characters have for getting involved in the cult and following its teachings beyond the limits of sanity. For me, it's a worthy extension of the lore without risking trampling the original themes, which is more than can be said for some of the spin-off movies. Yes, I'm looking at you "what if Cenobites but also a cautionary tale about getting too into an MMO," Hellraiser: Hellworld.

Like any self-respecting church, it has a "very arch, Sander Cohen-esque" prophet, Bruno. His character was one area that the development team worked closely with Barker on to stay authentic to the world of Hellraiser.

"He’s an extravagant, unhinged artist, and we went back and forth on quite how campy he could be,” says De Fault. “We knew we wanted him to be a ‘fun’ villain, compared to the very serious Marlowe and the Cenobites, but it was important to Clive that he remained just on the right side of believability.

"It made me realize that despite the inherent campiness and fun to be found in the kinda scrappy B-movie originals, the world of Hellraiser remains a very sincere thing to its creator, and by extension, to us.”

From the earliest trailers, it was very clear that Hellraiser: Revival was going further than most games would ever dare. "It was an unofficial goal of the team to be banned, unrated, or restricted at least somewhere in the world as one barometer of whether we’d done our jobs right,” De Fault reveals.

"But in a video game, it shouldn’t be enough to have the player simply see taboo things; it’s necessary to get them to perform taboo acts too. So we require the player to engage in extreme violence, to engage in sexual play, and just generally to stick their hands in a bunch of very questionable places. This didn’t mean bucking traditional survival-horror mechanics necessarily, but it did mean making them more sensual, or disgusting, or making firm choices like the more intimate first-person perspective."

One of the missions involves a sex club owned by the Cenobite cult, while another has you hunting down sex toys (including a dildo that promises to "rearrange your guts") and a spanking scene. All very consensual and well-mannered, these sequences manage to walk the line between self-awareness and pure titillation, making total sense in the storyline with an unapologetic delight. I mean, of course a group obsessed with the heights of pleasure of pain would have a kink club; it's just good business sense. You know what they say: Do what you love and you'll never truly work a day in your life.

This mission is just one part of the game that allows you to feel like you’re engaging with the "forbidden experience" theme of Barker's work, and De Fault argues that this is why people read (or play) Hellraiser.

Asked if there were any scenes where the team had to hold back, De Fault references a sequence where, in an Aidan flashback, we see someone clearly… petting their trouser snake… to images of Sunny.

"It’s very clear what he’s doing, but if we’d made his actual genitals visible during this act, it would have almost certainly tipped our age ratings over a threshold and eliminated the game from sale in most places,” he says. “So we just arranged the room so that you can’t actually get around in front of him while he’s doing that.

"It’s a tiny tweak that doesn’t take away from the moment at all. In fact, the strong mental image you’re given is probably more unsettling than anything we could have made out of pixels!"

Between pushing boundaries and showing restraint to stay within the realms of a playable game, Saber Interactive has created something that gives the Pinhead partial a real chance to explore a new dimension of the Hellbound world. The fact that Clive Barker was providing guidance to the development team means that, when it comes to the Cenobite storytelling, Hellraiser: Revival honors his vision, rather than just milking his name for clout. It all makes for a satisfying take on what makes the Cenobite mythos so compelling and a worthwhile addition to the canon. Just maybe wait until Grandma has gone to bed before you fire up the console.

Hellraiser: Revival is out now, and you can check out what our reviewer made of it here.

She's been a professional nerd since 2006 when she got her start on Official PlayStation Magazine in the UK, and has since worked for GamesIndustry.Biz, Rolling Stone and GamesRadar. articles.title: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 Is Not The Disaster You’d Imagine
articles.summary: Modern Warfare 4 is the first Call of Duty since 2013 to launch on a Nintendo console. We played the campaign on Switch 2 and were pleasantly surprised by its performance.
articles.body:
Not since 2013’s Call of Duty: Ghosts launched on the Wii U has a mainline COD game appeared on a Nintendo console. 2026’s Modern Warfare 4 is breaking that 14-year dry spell by releasing on Switch 2, and I got to play a couple of missions from the campaign to see how it fares. I won’t lie, my expectations were low – Call of Duty is always on the cutting edge of graphics and performance, and Nintendo’s latest isn’t intentionally built for that. And yet, I came away pleasantly surprised by what Digital Legends, the Activision studio dedicated to this version of MW4, has achieved from a technical standpoint.

For my full review of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , I played on PC, which provided a useful benchmark for what the most ideal version of the game looks like. Of course, when placed side-by-side with the Switch 2 version, you’ll immediately notice the difference — it looks stunning on PC and runs like a dream, as you’d expect. But, shifting over to Switch 2 didn’t offend my eyes quite like I feared it would. Granted, the textures are nowhere near as detailed, with flat surfaces and faces smoothed over to give the impression of plasticine versions of the campaign’s characters. It's by no means a looker, but considering the reduced horsepower Nintendo’s latest console is working with, the gameplay itself was smooth, running at 30fps at 4K while docked. The campaign is locked at 30, while multiplayer will target 60.

That campaign framerate remained consistent, too, not even hitching or stuttering during some of the story’s most explosive moments — I deliberately made sure to capture part of a mission that showcases one of its most hectic sequences to test it out. You can check that gameplay out for yourself in the video above, but I was left impressed that a game which normally demands so much of the hardware it is being played on performed so well on the Switch 2. Yes, it's quite a visual downgrade when compared to the likes of PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X, but that comes with the territory. And if you’re solely a Nintendo owner who’s been locked out of Call of Duty for over a decade, you’re getting a version of Modern Warfare 4 that feels every bit as snappy as the series usually is, even if it’s a bit muddier than Nintendo’s own crisp visuals.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 - Campaign Review
articles.summary: Modern Warfare 4 may not have quite enough to be considered amongst the very best Call of Duty campaigns, but if it’s to be the end of this particular saga, then at least it's going out on a high note.
articles.body:
These are our impressions of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s campaign. Reviews of DMZ and multiplayer will follow.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's campaign has been set an unenviable task: tie the bow on a seven-year-long series of stories I’d politely describe as “uneven.” To its credit, it handles this challenge well, delivering a genuinely exciting string of missions that are great when they focus on what is new, rather than getting bogged down in the past. It’s the best Modern Warfare has been since its 2019 reboot by quite some distance, and a reminder of how good Call of Duty can be when the people making it are given time to cook.

This collection of blockbuster sequences that has clearly been built from the ground up as a single-player experience is in stark contrast when compared to 2023’s woeful Modern Warfare 3 campaign, arguably the low point of the entire series. A mishmash of multiplayer maps mixed with slivers of near-incomprehensible story, I don’t envy Infinity Ward having to pick up from where it left off. The studio has done about as good a job as it could, though, thanks to a smart structure which splits the two halves of this story until they inevitably collide, providing both variety in mission design and tone.

Captain Price has been at the centre of the Modern Warfare plot, and that doesn’t change too much here. Following the disastrous finale of MW3, he’s now on the run, acting as a lone wolf, wanted by the very people he used to work for. His half of the story is initially tied up in knots so twisted even Alfred Borden would have trouble with them. Infinity Ward’s answer? Take a machete to much of it and kill off any characters introduced in the past two games that it deems superfluous. It’s almost an admission of guilt over how poorly these people were handled in the past, but it does give a sense of finality to this seemingly saga-ending chapter.

A tale of string-pullers and warmongers, Price’s story takes place over the course of five days in the run-up to the North Korean invasion of South Korea (plenty more on that in a moment). The former SAS captain has the blinkers on for his nemesis Makarov and whoever his boss may be. It’s fair to say that the Russian terrorist is not close to being the well-developed threat from the original Modern Warfare 2, which feels like a wasted opportunity to revive a famous villain. In his place steps Mads Mikkelsen’s The Archer.

For the most part, Price’s chapters of the story play like a Bond movie, packed full of parkour escapes, car chases, and stealthy infiltrations. Mikkelsen’s casting only reinforces this feeling, and while he’s classically unsettling in his performance, his character was never given quite enough screen time for me to grow a connection with him. As such, while the missions that make up Price’s side of the story are fun, it comes across as the weaker half. Infinity Ward clearly wants Price to be the strongest emotional bond to the player and for his personal vendettas to feel like our own, but, in truth, many more of the missions are dedicated to the Korean conflict. Incidentally, this is also where I found a lot more of the engaging storytelling to be found.

MW4’s 16 missions took me around the world as well as back and forth in time. The Korean invasion takes place in the “present day” as I followed a squad of soldiers from the moment war is sparked to its conclusion, while we switch back to Price every now and then as he hunts for whoever is behind the plot in the preceding week. These time shifts also allow for a clever mixture between traditional military missions and behind-enemy-lines ingenuity. For example, an early level has you fistfighting and gun-fu-ing your way through a New York nightclub as Price puts on his best John Wick impression. The next, you’ll be holding off paratroopers on the streets of Seoul armed with a mortar. While the Korean sections are generally louder and more traditional boots-on-the-ground “Call of Duty” in their approach, it came somewhat as a surprise to me that it managed to build such a strong connection to its playable character.

There’s an endearing nature to Young Mazino's Park Hyun Jun. Just as Farah did in 2019’s reboot, he gives an emotional anchor to the story that offsets the gruff military types nicely. The same can be said for his whole squad, a mixture of Korean and US soldiers who maintain a well-balanced mixture of levity and seriousness. Their bonds rooted me in its events well, and I actually cared what happened to them by the end. In general, I found the Korean side of things much more compelling and ended up caring about the likes of Park, his friend Jae, and their northern counterpart, Ko, a lot more. While Mikkelsen’s The Archer can come across as a moustache-twirling, nuclear weapon-wielding caricature at times, MW4 actually does a good job of bringing depth to the North Korean threat instead of painting each and every one of its leaders and people following their orders in one shade of evil.

The general direction of the story may not surprise you, but there are some engaging character moments that the past couple of Modern Warfare installments have desperately lacked. One such moment happens during one of the campaign’s standout missions: Stranded. As is the way these days, Call of Duty is now an interconnected beast, so this particular mission actually gives you a taste of MW4’s DMZ extraction mode as it takes you deep behind enemy lines. Due to your stranded nature, you have to go out into the wild and forage for ways to rebuild your arsenal by raiding outposts or heading to mystery markers on the map, then head back to the safety of your basement hideout to craft new equipment. What could so easily come across as a glorified, crowbarred tutorial does actually fit in and play around with the larger story in interesting ways.

Tasked with three main objectives to complete in any order you choose across a large snowy map, Stranded embraces freedom of approach as few other missions do. You could fast travel between the three key locations and move on with the story quickly if you’d like, or spend a couple of hours unlocking each of its snow-covered secrets, ranging from exotic weaponry to keypad-based puzzles to solve. It’s an evolution of Black Ops 6’s Phantom Pain-inspired open zone mission, trading in the sand for a much cooler climate that I enjoyed skulking around with my thermal-scoped sniper rifle. It’s elegantly folded into the campaign, too, making each of its chosen mechanics make narrative sense while also being very fun to play through.

This expansive chapter was the standout mission across the roughly seven hours it took me to complete the campaign, alongside Korea’s answer to D-Day – opening with a beach landing from hell where Infinity Ward’s phenomenal sound design gets to shine – and an airfield escape in which you can dynamically switch characters at will to hold off your attackers. The latter contains a great sense of spectacle that felt like pure Call of Duty at its core. These huge-scale operations are often the highlight, with the amount of moving parts at times simply astonishing. It’s a full-blown campaign crafted to be played like one, not a hodgepodge of other modes where the story feels held together with sticky tape. A sweet relief when compared to what preceded it three years prior. That being said, while the quality of the missions is consistently very good, there isn’t a genuine all-timer here to rival the likes of All Ghillied Up or Clean House, either.

That consistency only stumbles once or twice, usually when forcing you into some unforgiving stealth segments or asking you to engage in its imprecise counter-based melee system. First-person thumping can be disorienting at the best of times, and it's not done particularly well here. This is made even more frustrating by the fact that it often rears its head during some of the story’s key moments, meaning having to retry these brawls lessens the impact of what should feel like emotional hammer blows. Rest assured, these are rare occasions, though. For the most part, I enjoyed the mixture of new ideas being blended with age-old Call of Duty staples. Chopper gunner raids, night vision ambushes, and explosive tank sections. They all still hit the mark. Especially when soundtracked by some fantastically emphatic music at times — the Korean battles in particular are scored with some adrenaline-fuelled electronic orchestrations.

The gunplay is refined, packing the sort of punch we’ve come to expect from Infinity Ward, but still shouldn’t be taken for granted. Movement is slick, being able to transition from a sprint into a slide, before mounting onto a pillar and peeking around the corner to pop a head peeking out of cover. No, enemy AI may not be the smartest, but that doesn’t mean you should play them for fools. Even on regular difficulty, get a little cocky and opt for the run-and-gun approach and your health bar won’t last too long. Managing your ammo, armour plates, and cover is needed, especially towards the campaign’s latter missions. Enemy variety may be limited, but a few heavily armoured brutes caused me quite a bit of trouble when trying to stay out of the blast of their shotguns in some tight underground tunnels. Nothing a few stolen explosive shells of my own couldn’t eventually sort out, though.

Modern Warfare 4 made me feel something for the series again. A consistently strong set of missions manages to juggle a bloated cast successfully, saying goodbye to familiar faces while building impressive bonds with new ones. Its expansive behind-enemy-lines mission that borrows most of its ideas from the DMZ mode is a real highlight, as is whenever its blockbuster ambitions are fulfilled and full-throttle battles break out. It may not have quite enough to be considered amongst the very best Call of Duty campaigns, but if it’s to be the end of this particular saga, then at least Modern Warfare is going out on a high note.

articles.title: James McAvoy Reveals He Once Pitched a Young Picard Star Trek Show
articles.summary: James McAvoy revealed he pitched a Picard Star Trek show that would have seen him yet again star as a young Patrick Stewart.
articles.body:
James McAvoy revealed he pitched a Picard Star Trek show that would have seen him yet again star as a young Patrick Stewart.

The Split and X-Men actor opened up about his love for Stewart's time in the Star Trek universe during a conversation on Happy, Sad, Confused . He said it's something those overseeing the sci-fi franchise "nearly did," and although it never came to be, it's still an idea he's excited about to this day.

Instead of stemming directly from his love for Star Trek or even Stewart's Next Generation captain, Jean-Luc Picard, it sounds like McAvoy's idea for a limited series also came from his connection to Stewart himself.

"Mutiny on the Stargazer: That was a whole idea I had that I pitched the Star Trek people, as well. Nearly did it," the actor teased. When pressed for an explanation, he said, "I've got a whole story about an early Picard. I mean, all I really want to do in my career is play young versions of Patrick."

That, of course, is a reference to McAvoy's time spent playing Charles Xavier in films like X-Men: First Class , Days of Future Past, Apocalypse, and Dark Phoenix. It's a character made famous in the movie world by Stewart's aged-up portrayal in the original 2000s X-Men trilogy, and considering most seem to think McAvoy nailed the part in his follow-ups, a part as a young Picard could definitely make sense, too.

Alas, the Picard prequel never took off. The actor explained that he developed a whole story for what would have been a one-off season of TV that he still loves to this day, but for now, at least, his time as a young Stewart will be limited to the Marvel universe.

"It was like a one-off standalone season when he took over as captain of the Stargazer, and what actually happened and the secret he's been holding his entire career," McAvoy said. "I just pitched it to them, talking to them, and they were well into it, but we had logistical issues, and we couldn't do it. But I love that story. I just go to bed and think about it at night."

Star Trek fans have already seen plenty from the life of Jean-Luc Picard. The character was first introduced as the captain of the USS Enterprise when he was played by Stewart in The Next Generation, but you don't have to be a die-hard fan of the franchise to know he's one of its most important characters. Despite this, the parts of his story we do know are mostly from later in his career, with his debut show – as well as projects like First Contact, Insurrection, and Nemesis – fleshing out the timeline further. The more focused follow-up series, Star Trek: Picard , premiered in 2020 and finished in 2023.

The Best Star Trek Series of the Modern Era (and the Worst)

While McAvoy's story for a younger version of the character remains on the cutting room floor, you can check out what Stewart had to say about his hopes for a new movie . You can also read IGN's Picard Season 3 9/10 review .

The X2 Superstrike features Logitech's new Haptic Inductive Trigger System (HITS). Instead of physical (and clicky) microswitches, the buttons now use electromagnetic sensors. You'll still feel the click, but it's coming from the haptic motor's rumble, not from the actual click itself. As a side effect, the buttons are quieter, so you can use it at night without bothering anyone, and fewer moving parts means there's less chance for mechanical components to wear out.

Another advantage of electromagnetic sensors is the increased amount of customizability. The X2 Superstrike has tunable action and reset points. You can adjust your click's travel distance, both during the press and the reset. Choose from ten actuation points and five rapid-trigger reset points. This is not dissimilar to the latest generation gaming keyboards with magnetic switches, but it's now translated over to a gaming mouse.

articles.title: Nvidia App Update Adds Support for Agent Control, but Some Users are Warning to Turn It Off
articles.summary: It's no secret that Nvidia loves its AI, and fresh off of launching RTX Spark – the new chipset for Agentic laptops – the Nvidia app now has a toggle that'll let AI agents control it. The problem is that it's turned on by default.
articles.body:
It's no secret that Nvidia loves its AI, and fresh off of launching RTX Spark – the new chipset for Agentic laptops – the Nvidia app now has a toggle that'll let AI agents control it. The problem is that it's turned on by default.

Nvidia added the option in Nvidia App 11.0.9.565 on October 13. In that update's patch notes, it says, "Nvidia App includes a local MCP server (Model Context Protocol) that lets a compatible AI agent control the Nvidia App using natural-language requests. This means your AI assistant like Hermes, OpenClaw or Perplexity can see your installed games and apply optimal settings, or enable Shadowplay to record gameplay, all through simple conversation."

It's not terribly surprising that Nvidia has added this option to the Nvidia app; after all, it did just debut its RTX Spark platform, which is built entirely around AI agents, so it makes sense that the Nvidia App would let users hook those agents in. But the setting isn't exclusive to RTX Spark systems and shows up for anyone who installs the latest version of the app.

And, of course, some people are upset and worried about the security implications of letting an AI agent control their graphics cards .

Silent Hill: Ascension cinematic director Agustin Cordes tweeted about the update , saying, "PSA: Can confirm that the Nvidia app is automatically updating and has *enabled by default* a setting which allows AI agents to control the app with very permissive rights. Besides the obnoxious privacy invasion and lame AI features, it's a high security risk you may not want."

Meanwhile, a swath of fans quoted his post, like user TheAcidBurns3, who says, "Please pay attention to this. You do NOT want your graphics card being accessed like this!"

User DATGUYCOOP, who appears to be a cybersecurity professional, urged most laypeople to turn the feature off, saying, "Just gonna say turn this feature off. Trust from the cyber security man. If you work with AI agents, its a good way to add filtering and protections and secondary checks, but to the common folk, it adds a threat vector that is better off closed. Now, there [are] no reported exploits as of yet, but it's new and adds possible connector that could mayhaps do something later, so just turn it off."

The problem really seems to be that the Nvidia App update turns the setting on by default, which is almost a surefire way to get people to hate any given feature in a tech product. Nvidia isn't new to letting AI systems and agents mess with your graphics card; after all, the company revealed Project G-Assist at Computex 2024, which was essentially an LLM that helped you manage GPU settings like clock speeds, fan curves, and more.

I've reached out to Nvidia about the security implications of this new Nvidia App update, and will update this article if a response is given. But regardless of what Team Green says, it's unlikely that this option is going anywhere any time soon. So, if you don't want your GPU driver to have a door open to AI agents, either install your graphics driver manually or turn off the setting by going into the Nvidia App, hit Settings, then scrolling down to 'AI Agents and App Connections' and disabling 'Allow Agents to control Nvidia App.'

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: MTG Darkhold Destiny Arcanum Bundle: What's Inside and Is It Worth The Price Tag?
articles.summary: MTG Marvel Darkhold Destiny Arcanum Bundle features exclusive alt-art promo cards and booster packs. Here is a breakdown of what is inside and if it is worth the $100 preorder price tag.
articles.body:
Preorders are now open for Magic: The Gathering's next Marvel crossover, Darkhold Destiny . Amazon has already listed the Darkhold Destiny Arcanum Bundle for $99.99 , sold directly by the retailer, which is quickly becoming one of the most popular items from the new set.

For comparison, trading card marketplace TCGplayer is asking $200 for the same bundle , meaning Amazon is $100.01 cheaper. On the other hand, you shouldn’t take TCGplayer’s lowest price as the best listing available on the site in the short term, as there are currently only two sellers at this time; we expect more to appear as time goes on.

In the meantime, the Darkhold Destiny Arcanum Bundle has an interesting collection content-wise, and whether it’s worth the price tag or not more or less depends on what you’re looking for.

What's Inside the Darkhold Destiny Arcanum Bundle?

Along with a Collector Booster (alt-art Arcanum promo cards and Full-Art Lands), you’ll also get eight regular Booster Packs inside Darkhold Destiny’s Arcanum Bundle.

If you’re the type of Magic: The Gathering collector who usually likes going after the fancier treatments — like source-material cards, silver foil versions, and Midnight Raised Foils, that’s already a nice extra bang for your hundred bucks.

On the other hand, don’t go into this thinking you’re guaranteed one of the rarest pulls from the get-go, as the headliner Mythic Rares only have a 1% chance of appearing in Collector Boosters.

Personally, I think it’s the promos that will make this one more worth grabbing. You get three altogether: one traditional foil Mythic Rare, and two of six traditional foil promos — the latter being Arcanum cards with alternate art that’s exclusive to the bundle.

The remaining extras are 30 basic lands, including ten full-art Bifrost lands (five foil and five non-foil), an oversized Spindown life counter and a dedicated storage box.

As for Darkhold Destiny itself, first impressions so far make it seem like it’s a definite Magic: The Gathering worth grabbing if you were of a fan of the earlier Marvel Super Heroes, or you’re simply catching up and want to try new crossovers.

The story behind it is another interesting one, with Dormammu and Hela using a page of the Darkhold to tear through realities and spread ‘arcane nightmares across the multiverse’, as Wizards of the Coast puts it; all standard comic book-esque fun.

As for value in terms of the Darkhold Destiny Arcanum Bundle, however, Amazon also lists the regular nine-pack Bundle for $69.99 , whilst Draft Night costs $119.99 with 12 boosters and a Collector Booster. If you’re more after grabbing as many packs as possible, I’d advise those latter two being your top priority.

The regular Bundle does have its own mechanically unique Mythic Rare promo, though; it’s just not packing alternate-art cards and a Collector Booster like the Arcanum version.

Be that as it may, the Arcanum bundle is totally worth it if you want a good amount of packs and some exclusive foil promos to go with it — pretty much a must-buy for avid Magic collectors.

There are currently no other listings outside of Amazon’s $99.99 and TCGplayer’s $200 listings, though, so we’d advise grabbing the former whilst you can before it sells out if you’re keen.

Ben Williams – IGN freelance contributor with over 10 years of experience covering gaming, tech, film, TV, and anime. Follow him on Twitter/X @BenLevelTen .

articles.title: Keys for the Guardians in ALCS: The Four Horsemen of Game 4
articles.summary: Let's see how this could go
articles.body:
It's Friday and we have a big time ballgame tonight! And fortunately for me, I get to write ~before~ the game tonight instead of after! Through 3 games our Cleveland Guardians have scratched and clawed and clutched their way to a 2-1 series lead, but with 2 more wins necessary and more bad weather on the horizon, we are far from comfortable in this series.

Speaking of being uncomfortable and bad weather (the apocalypse?) on the horizon; a thought has dawned on me when thinking of the keys to Game 4. Four. 2024. The nickname of that bullpen was THE FOUR HORSEMEN. Cade, Gaddis, Herrin and of course, Death incarnate, he who shall not be named, made up for a record setting end of the bullpen en route to an ALCS birth. And while that was a great nickname for that quartet, I figure we can use that again today as we head into the storm and towards Game 4.

So, without further ado, the FOUR HORSEMEN OF GAME FOUR!

(The quotes are taken from the Book of Revelation 6: 1-8)

I heard one of the four living creatures saying with a voice like thunder, "Come and see." And I looked, and behold, a white horse. He who sat on it had a bow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering and to conquer.

Now, through this interpretation, one could go many directions. But considering who is still to come, I ruled Jose out (for now) and decided again to go with Steven Vogt… Most people won't consider the Manager for one of the keys to victory, but it needs to be said: he's pushed all the right buttons in these wins. When to pull a pitcher, which reliever to go to, the Halpin starts and pinch hitting Bailey, all thanks to Vogter making the right moves at the right time. He has helped us go from scrapping around .500c to conquering the #1 seed, and if we are to conquer again, we will need him to continue to make all the right moves. Whatever they may be…

Another horse, fiery red, went out. And it was granted to the one who sat on it to take peace from the earth, and that people should kill one another; and there was given to him a great sword.

Ok damn this is dark. But come on, is there anyone more ready to lead us into War than Jose Ramirez?! Especially in this interpretation where, he does make the other team want to pull their own hair out as he beats you in every way possible. He is the spiritual leader on this team, and it has never been more obvious than it has been over the last 10 days. When he performs, we rally, when he doesn't, we sink. For example;

ALDS G3 W: 2-4, 2 RBI, 2 R, BB, 2B, 3B, SB, a classic Jose run created (2B, SB, take home on an infield in FC)

ALDS G4 W: 2-5, 3 RBI including the 2run HR to take the lead that gave us home we were gonna win this thing

ALCS G1 W: 3-5, RBI & a steal attempt that got Caminero to move out of the way of an Adell 2 run single

ALCS G2 L: 1-4, but a huge error that cost us 3 runs and well as a mental error that he knows he's better than

Clearly, you see the trend here. When he performs, we Win, when he doesn't? We are left for dead… Jose Ramirez is our Horsemen Leader into the ALCS War.

So I looked, and behold, a black horse, and he who sat on it had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the oil and the wine.

Ok so the translation kinda gets lost for this one but the point here is that the Third Horsemen is responsible for famine, starvation, and going hungry. And if the Guardians are to take Game 4, they will face this head on in the form of Nick Martinez. Who is somewhat the ambassador of starvation, aka, lack of runs.

In 2 starts vs Cleveland this season, Martinez has absolutely dominated… he's thrown 13 shutout innings, scattering 7 H, 1 BB while striking out 9. Now, he hasn't been the same pitcher since those first two incredible months, but I hardly think that applies here. With their season on the line, Cash and the Rays are gonna lean heavily on Martinez to be far more than the JAG he had been earlier in his career, and continue to be the All Star Frontline Starter he's become. The best way to get to him is getting on base, threatening early, turning the lineup over for a 3rd time thru by the 5th so that Cash will be forced to go to the 'pen early. Threaten, Turn it over, Force a move or score some runs.

Hopefully we have adjusted, or be prepared to be starved!

And the name of him who sat on it was Death, and Hades followed with him. And power was given to them over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword, with hunger, with death, and by the beasts of the earth.

I could be wrong but that's literally what the narrator says as Cade walks by you at any given point. And there is no better way to describe your Closer than DEATH.

Cade has been phenomenal this run. He's pitched in every victory, and will continue to be leaned upon for as many outs as he can give. In the 7 games he's pitched, he's thrown 9 innings, striking out 13 while giving up 1 run, a meaningless Solo homer up 5. The Guardians have made their plan simple, get the lead after the 5th and its "operation: bullpen", which will end unceremoniously with Cade striking out three more victims en route to total annihilation.

So there it is, the plan to victory through the eyes of the 4 Horsemen of Game 4. Vogt needs to make the right moves and continue to pull the correct levers in attempt to conquer, Jose must lead us into War thru his patented style of play, both must keep us from starving at the hands of Nick Martinez, and finally, get to the 8th with a lead and eventually hand it over to Cade Smith. Who will slam the door shut and kill any chance at life.
